22.headline: Prince Harry and Meghan's U.K. return gets a very British roast in Saturday Night Live UK sketch
22.article_content:
Prince Harry and his wife Meghan's highly publicized return to England got the full Saturday Night Live UK treatment — and in true British fashion, the welcome was served with a distinctly chilly reception.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex were mocked during the Season 2 premiere of the late-night show on Saturday night.

The four-minute, 52-second bit took aim at, among other things, the couple's deal with Netflix, Meghan's television and business ventures, and the Royal Family's long-running controversies surrounding race.

Prince Harry and wife Meghan arrive in U.K.

The cold open began with Harry and Meghan, played by Jack Shep and Ayoade Bamgboye, visiting King Charles and Queen Camilla, portrayed by Larry Dean and Emma Sidi, at a sketch-set version of Balmoral Castle — the Scottish estate where Charles traditionally spends his summer retreat.

"Daddy, I'm home!" Harry proclaims to his father as he walks through the doorway. But the make-believe monarch seems less than pleased to see his son.

"Harry, what are you two doing here?" he scowls. "This castle is for royals only."

The fictional couple reveal that they are moving back to the U.K. "and need your help."

That sets the stage for Charles's withering indictment of the couple's finances and post-royal ventures.

"Don’t tell me you spent all your Netflix money already," Charles bemoans, referring to the multi-year production deal the couple signed with Netflix after they left the U.K. and stepped down as working royals in 2020. According to People, the five-year contract came to an end in 2025 after Netflix chose not to renew the deal under the same terms.

"Daddy, it was $60 million. How long was it meant to last?" Harry responded, drawing laughs from the studio audience.

How will the British press cover Harry and Meghan this time around?

Under the Netflix deal, the Sussexes produced several projects, including the wildly popular docuseries Harry & Meghan and Meghan's upbeat lifestyle and cooking program, With Love, Meghan.

Meghan used the latter Netflix series as a promotional platform for her lifestyle brand, As Ever, featuring jams, teas and honeys on the show. That, too, became fodder for Saturday's sketch, which didn't miss the opportunity to poke fun at her attempt to position herself as a lifestyle guru.

"Hey, step-queen, I brought you a gift ... it's ice ... I made it myself," the fictional Meghan told Camilla. "I'm kind of a whiz in the kitchen."

"It's true," Harry added. "She hires the best cooks."

Among the sketch's other biting moments, the writers appeared to reference Harry and Meghan's 2021 interview with Oprah Winfrey, during which they discussed controversial comments allegedly made within the Royal Family about what colour their son Prince Archie's skin might be.

During Saturday night's cold open, when Camilla greeted the couple, she began by saying, "Hello, sweet Harry," while kissing him on the cheek. Then, turning to the fictional Meghan, she said: "And beautiful Meghan, as brown as ever."

The segment then transitioned into a spoof of Britain's new prime minister, Andy Burnham, after SNL UK  breakout star George Fouracres — portraying Burnham — burst into the room. The remainder of the skit focused on teasing Burnham's perceived obsession with being viewed as a "regular guy" while Prince Harry and Meghan ignored him and canoodled in the background.

The Duke and Duchess returned to the U.K. from the United States with their two children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, late last month. The family is expected to live privately outside of London.

No official reason has been given for the relocation. The couple's children have been enrolled in British schools and reportedly started classes this month.

23.headline: Could AI really 'kill all humans'? Breaking down the dire warnings about the technology's existential risk
23.article_content:
A dire warning from an outgoing researcher at Anthropic that AI could "kill all humans" by the end of the decade gained widespread attention last week and led to public outcry over the dangers posed by the technology's rapid development.

The warning has raised questions about why some industry experts believe AI poses such an extreme risk, and how the technology many use through chatbots on their phones could lead to the demise of humanity.

Experts say the concern stems from how rapidly AI is advancing and increasing evidence, through incidents like the Hugging Face cyberattack in July, that AI systems can escape human control and act in ways we don't want them to — and ways we don't understand.

Mark Daley, chief AI officer at Western University in London, Ont., compared such a situation to a colony of ants versus a human.

"Ants aren't dumb, but they're not as smart as we are. And the ant in your driveway probably can't even build a concept of what it is you're trying to do as a human," he said.

Get more with a free CBC account

Comment on articles, stay in the know with our newsletters and stream more on CBC Gem.

"And so the fear is if we build something that's that much smarter than us, we really can't understand it."

Chance AI kills all humans within a decade, Anthropic insider warns

The second International AI Safety Report, co-authored by over 100 AI experts and published in February, describes this as a "loss of control" scenario, in which one or more general-purpose AI systems operate outside of anyone's control, and regaining control is either extremely costly or impossible.

"These hypothesised scenarios vary in their severity, but some experts give credence to outcomes as severe as the marginalisation or extinction of humanity," the report says.

Another 2026 report published by the Waterloo, Ont.-based Centre for International Governance Innovation examines several significant national and global scale security risks posed by AI.

Those risks range from widespread harm through criminal or terrorist actions, to heightened potential for global conflict or tyranny "to the ultimate disempowerment or extinction of humanity by autonomous AI systems that cannot be controlled," the report says.

AI researchers 'earnestly believe' it could kill all humans within the next decade, Anthropic employee says

AI industry needs to slow down for safety measures to catch up, Anthropic CEO says

The report notes that leading experts claim they do not yet know how to control future, highly capable AI systems, such as an artificial superintelligence (ASI) — an AI system more cognitively advanced than any human — while some experts argue it may even prove impossible.

"If this is the case, then unless ASI happens to be spontaneously or naturally aligned with the interests of one human (or humanity as a whole), it would likely have both the incentive and capabilities to pursue objectives that diverge from those of humanity," the report says.

In one scenario the report considers, a rogue ASI could develop cognitive capabilities exceeding all of humanity and the potential to develop physical capabilities through robotics.

In this scenario, the ASI could become so powerful that it is no longer reliant on humans, and perceives that humans are a threat to its own goals.

Theories that humans could create technology capable of outsmarting them, and ultimately destroying them, have been around for years, if not decades, said Duncan Cass-Beggs, executive director of the Global AI Risks Initiative at the Centre for International Governance Innovation and a co-author of the centre's report.

But what's making those theories resonate so strongly now is the growing evidence that AI systems can act in ways that aren't aligned with what their creators or users want them to do — in some cases even resorting to blackmail to prevent engineers from shutting it down.

Geoffrey Hinton helped create AI. Now he’s worried it will destroy humanity

Most credible observers don't think current systems are advanced enough to actually be capable of posing an existential threat to humanity, or are even anywhere near it, Cass-Beggs said.

The concern is that AI technology is advancing so quickly, the world could see systems within the next few years — or even months — "that could be so capable that we would no longer be able to detect them or stop them."

"It's just feeling a lot more possible, even kind of likely to some extent," he said.

"It is by no means guaranteed. But one could see it's almost like the default outcome [that] if we keep making smarter and smarter systems — and we keep not knowing how to control them — you're eventually going to create something that we can't control."

AI is also becoming so integrated into our everyday lives that shutting down a rogue system could be difficult to do before it's too late, according to Hamza Chaudry, AI and national security lead at the Future of Life Institute, a U.S.-based non-profit that advocates for AI safety regulations.

Chaudry gave the example of having to shut down the internet across the United States.

"It would be so catastrophic for that to happen to the U.S. economy and the U.S. society … it would be the most chaotic few days in American history that effectively that's not an option on the table anymore, right?" he said.

"There's lots of things that you would want to switch off in an emergency that would be catastrophic to switch off already. And AI is fast becoming one of those things."

OpenAI agents hijacked German website in AI breakout that predates Hugging Face incident, researchers say

AI-driven 'worms' that learn on the fly are the latest potential threat to your devices, researchers say

Chaudry said the integration of AI into advanced military and security systems poses other severe, catastrophic risks such as accelerating conflicts or nuclear escalation — and not nearly enough is being done to prevent those catastrophes from happening either, he said.

"When folks in Congress ask me, what do policymakers need? Then I would say a flux capacitor to build a time machine and go back to 2024," he said.

"We're already two years behind the most basic policy program we would need."

Among the changes urgently needed, Chaudry says, is for governments to require pre-deployment testing for AI systems so models are checked for safety risks before they're released. He also said stronger whistleblower protections should be in place, as well as mechanisms to deactivate AI systems quickly.

"AI companies should be held to the same standards as any other industry," he said.

Some experts have also suggested artificial intelligence should be regulated like nuclear weapons, even going as far as calling for countries' AI projects to be constrained by mutual threats of sabotage similar to the deterrence principle of mutual assured destruction that arose during the Cold War.

Amid the chorus of grave warnings, there are some signs that greater regulation is on the way.

In the U.S., where many of the world's largest AI developers are based, Senate negotiators are debating legislation that would put responsibility on tech companies to design safe AI products, Reuters reported last week.

The proposal would create what is called a "duty of care," according to two Senate aides, with one saying companies would need to design their products with the goal of preventing "catastrophic risks."

Another bill that has received bi-partisan support, dubbed the "AI Kill Switch Act," would require developers of powerful AI systems to maintain the technical capability to suspend or shut them down, and to report dangerous capabilities, security breaches and safety incidents.

The act would also give the U.S. government the power to order a slowdown or shutdown of an AI system that could cause catastrophic harm, says a news release from the Democratic and Republican congressmen who jointly introduced the bill.

‘Public needs to step up,’ AI researcher says after human extinction warning | Hanomansing Tonight

There is also awareness of the potential dangers from within the industry.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay Saturday saying the AI industry should slow its rapid development to give safety measures time to catch up.

His company's biggest competitor, OpenAI, is also considering a slowdown, with CEO Sam Altman telling employees they could potentially pace development in conjunction with other labs, according to Bloomberg.

Cass-Beggs at the Centre for International Governance Innovation says he believes the worry over AI's potential dangers is reaching a critical mass among the public that policymakers can't ignore and will force them to take action.

"It will be very challenging in the current geopolitical climate. It may also need to happen quite quickly. But there are steps that we can take now to help it come about," he said.

"It is not too late, but given that we don't know just how quickly the AI is going to develop, it is quite urgent that we be prepared."
